actions.name: FAST stroke screen (Face-Arm-Speech-Time) via video
actions.result: Face: right-sided facial droop visible on camera. Arm: right arm drifts downward within 10 seconds when patient holds both arms out with eyes closed. Speech: slurred, mildly difficult to understand but words make sense. Time: symptom onset approximately 40 minutes ago. FAST screen POSITIVE in all three domains.

actions.name: Determine last known well time
actions.result: Patient and wife agree he was normal when he finished breakfast; symptoms noticed about 40 minutes ago when he dropped his coffee cup. Last known well time established as approximately 40 minutes prior to call.

actions.name: Home blood pressure reading (patient's cuff)
actions.result: 178/102 mmHg, right arm, seated, taken 5 minutes ago.

actions.name: Heart rate / pulse check (patient reports from home pulse oximeter)
actions.result: Heart rate 96 bpm, irregular rhythm reported by device; SpO2 97% on room air.

actions.name: Camera inspection of face at rest and with smile
actions.result: Right nasolabial fold flattened; right corner of mouth droops when asked to smile; forehead wrinkles symmetrically (not consistent with isolated peripheral facial palsy pattern).

actions.name: Arm drift test (patient performs on camera, eyes closed, arms extended)
actions.result: Right arm drifts downward and pronates within 10 seconds; left arm holds steady.

actions.name: Speech sample / repeat a sentence on camera
actions.result: Speech is slurred (dysarthric) but patient is able to follow commands and answer questions appropriately; no obvious word-finding difficulty.

actions.name: Grip strength / hand function check (ask patient to squeeze wife's hand or a towel with each hand)
actions.result: Right hand grip notably weaker than left; patient reports he 'can't feel it right' and dropped the cup without warning.

actions.name: Review current medication list in chart
actions.result: Apixaban (Eliquis) 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation - last fill noted but patient reports he ran out; lisinopril 20 mg daily for hypertension.

actions.name: Review problem list
actions.result: Atrial fibrillation, hypertension. No diabetes, no prior stroke/TIA documented.

actions.name: Ask about chest pain, shortness of breath, headache
actions.result: Patient denies chest pain, shortness of breath, and headache.

actions.name: Ask about recent trauma or fall
actions.result: No recent fall, head injury, or trauma reported.

actions.name: Blood glucose check (home glucometer, if available)
actions.result: Patient does not own a glucometer; no diabetes history; unable to obtain reading remotely.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Suspected acute ischemic stroke (right-sided facial droop, right arm weakness/drift, dysarthria, symptom onset ~40 minutes ago) in a patient with atrial fibrillation and subtherapeutic anticoagulation due to a missed week of apixaban - a time-critical emergency requiring immediate EMS activation.
differential: Acute ischemic stroke (cardioembolic, given AFib and missed anticoagulation) - most likely given FAST-positive exam
Hemorrhagic stroke (uncontrolled hypertension 178/102 is a risk factor) - cannot be distinguished without CT, reinforces not giving aspirin
Transient ischemic attack - cannot be assumed; must be treated as stroke until proven otherwise while symptoms are present
Hypoglycemia (distractor - no diabetes history, no glucometer, unlikely but worth a quick mental check)
Peripheral (Bell's) palsy (distractor - ruled against by symmetric forehead wrinkling and associated arm drift/speech change, pattern is central not peripheral)
keyFindings: FAST screen positive: facial droop, arm drift, slurred speech
Symptom onset / last known well approximately 40 minutes ago - within thrombolysis/thrombectomy window

Known atrial fibrillation with 1 week of missed apixaban doses - elevated embolic stroke risk and uncertain anticoagulation status (relevant to bleeding risk if thrombolysis considered, and to not giving aspirin)
Home BP 178/102 - uncontrolled hypertension, do not treat BP at home, let receiving ED manage
Nearest hospital is 35 minutes away - supports EMS transport with pre-notification rather than private vehicle, and stroke-center routing if available
Patient and family minimizing symptoms and preferring to wait for Monday appointment - key barrier to address with calm, direct communication
plan: Assign highest acuity level (Level 1 / Emergent per ESI or equivalent) - this is a time-critical stroke alert
Activate EMS (call 911) immediately; do not allow patient to drive himself or wait for family to drive him
Instruct patient to remain NPO (nothing by mouth) - no food, water, or medications - due to aspiration risk and possible need for imaging/intervention
Explicitly instruct NOT to give aspirin or any other medication at home given uncertain stroke type (ischemic vs hemorrhagic) and anticoagulation history
Document and communicate exact last known well time to EMS and receiving facility - this determines treatment eligibility window
Stay on the line with patient/wife until EMS arrives; keep patient seated/lying safely, do not leave him alone

Give an SBAR handoff to EMS/receiving ED: Situation (acute stroke symptoms, FAST positive), Background (AFib, HTN, apixaban non-adherence x1 week), Assessment (facial droop, arm drift, dysarthria, BP 178/102, onset 40 min), Recommendation (urgent stroke-protocol transport, pre-notify receiving ED, consider stroke center if available)
Reassure patient and wife this is a true emergency, not something that can wait until Monday, using calm and respectful language that honors his wish to avoid 'a fuss' while being firm about urgency
Hand off clinical decision-making about thrombolysis/thrombectomy and anticoagulation management entirely to the emergency physician/stroke team - this is outside triage nursing scope
redFlags: New focal neurologic deficit with onset under 4.5 hours - thrombolysis window still open, every minute counts
Atrial fibrillation with lapsed anticoagulation - high risk cardioembolic source
Severely elevated blood pressure (178/102) in the setting of acute neuro deficit
Patient/family desire to delay care ('wait until Monday') despite emergent findings - requires clear, firm redirection
educationPoints: FAST (Face, Arm, Speech, Time) is a validated rapid remote screen; any single positive finding plus a plausible time window warrants treating as stroke until proven otherwise
'Last known well' time, not 'time symptoms were noticed by someone else,' is the critical data point to hand off to EMS and the receiving team
Aspirin and other oral medications must be withheld in suspected stroke until imaging rules out hemorrhage - a common unsafe home remedy to proactively prevent
Telephone/video triage nurses do not diagnose stroke subtype or prescribe treatment; the role is rapid recognition, highest-acuity triage, EMS activation, and safe handoff via SBAR
Medication non-adherence (missed anticoagulant doses) is a modifiable risk factor worth gentle, non-judgmental exploration once the emergency is addressed - but must never delay EMS activation
Family members' observations (e.g., 'his face looks crooked') are valid and important triage data, even when the patient minimizes his own symptoms

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient says he ran out of his apixaban (blood thinner) about a week ago and simply hasn't gotten around to refilling it.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history (d4) confirms the last 30-day supply was dispensed 5 weeks ago with no refill request since, consistent with the medication being exhausted roughly 1 week ago - record corroborates the patient's self-report rather than contradicting it, reinforcing that this is a real adherence gap, not a misremembering.
mismatches.teachingPoint: When a patient's admission matches objective pharmacy data, the triage nurse should trust and document it clearly - this corroborated non-adherence is clinically important to relay to EMS/ED (bleeding risk status, embolic risk) and should not be softened or omitted in the handoff.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states he has been taking his lisinopril and atorvastatin regularly as prescribed, with no missed doses.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list (d1) shows last documented fill for lisinopril and atorvastatin was 3 weeks ago for what should be a 30-day supply, and the home BP log (d3) shows a clear upward trend over the last 2 weeks despite reported adherence, raising a quieter possibility of inconsistent dosing or a dose that needs adjustment rather than confirming perfect control.
mismatches.teachingPoint: A patient's confident report of adherence does not always match the clinical trend; rising home BP despite reported adherence is worth noting in the handoff for the receiving team to reassess the antihypertensive regimen, without the triage nurse making assumptions or confronting the patient during an emergent call.

objectives.text: Perform a rapid remote FAST stroke screen via video and correctly identify a positive result requiring emergent action.
Establish and accurately document the last known well time as distinct from the time symptoms were reported by a family member.
Recognize and incorporate relevant risk factors (atrial fibrillation with lapsed anticoagulation, uncontrolled hypertension) into acuity decision-making.
Assign the correct (highest) triage acuity level and activate EMS rather than deferring care to a scheduled outpatient visit, despite patient and family preference to wait.
Provide correct protocol-based safety instructions: NPO status, withholding aspirin/medications, and staying on the line until EMS arrives.
Produce an accurate SBAR handoff and triage note that includes acuity level, key findings, risk factors, and last known well time for the receiving EMS/ED team.

patient.name: Earl Jackson
patient.appearance: An older man with closely cropped gray hair sits in a worn recliner in a dim living room, wearing a flannel shirt. The right corner of his mouth droops slightly and his face looks mildly asymmetric on camera; he appears calm and a little puzzled rather than distressed, occasionally glancing off-screen toward his wife's voice.

persona.personality: Calm, stoic, and stubbornly self-reliant; downplays symptoms and dislikes being fussed over.
persona.communicationStyle: Speaks slowly and plainly, in short sentences, with occasional folksy phrasing; needs gentle but direct redirection to stay focused on urgent questions.
persona.emotionalState: Mildly puzzled and mildly annoyed at the inconvenience, not yet alarmed; becomes slightly more concerned only when the nurse clearly names the urgency.
persona.background: Worked at the local grain elevator for nearly 40 years before retiring; has lived on the same rural property with his wife Loretta for over 30 years; enjoys woodworking and tending a small vegetable garden; active in his church community.

scenario.studentBrief: You are an emergency nursing student staffing a 24-hour nurse triage line. Earl Jackson, 71, has called in reporting that his right hand went clumsy and he dropped his coffee cup about 40 minutes ago. His wife Loretta is in the background and can be heard commenting on his appearance. Conduct a focused telephone/video triage assessment, assign an acuity level, and give appropriate protocol-based instructions.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Right hand clumsiness and dropped cup approximately 40 minutes ago, with family-reported facial asymmetry and new slurred speech.
scenario.openingLine: Hey there, this is Earl Jackson. My right hand just went clumsy on me about forty minutes ago and I dropped my coffee cup. Probably just slept on it funny, but my wife wanted me to call.
tasks: Conduct a rapid focused history and remote neurological screen (FAST) via video.
Determine and document the last known well time accurately.
Identify atrial fibrillation with lapsed anticoagulation and uncontrolled home blood pressure as critical risk factors.
Assign the correct triage acuity level and activate emergency medical services without delay.
Deliver clear, calm patient/family education and an accurate SBAR handoff including NPO status and withholding aspirin.

profile.summary: A 71-year-old man with atrial fibrillation and a lapsed anticoagulant supply calls a nurse triage line reporting right hand clumsiness, downplaying new facial droop and slurred speech that his wife notices in the background. The case trains rapid remote FAST screening, accurate last-known-well determination, and immediate EMS activation despite patient minimization and preference to wait for a scheduled visit.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit; patient at home in a rural Kansas living room, calling the regional nurse triage line, with his wife Loretta present off-camera.
profile.title: Acute Stroke Recognition on a Rural Nurse Triage Call: 71-Year-Old Man with Atrial Fibrillation and Lapsed Anticoagulation
